# On Wandering Thought

There's something pleasant about writing without a destination in mind. No thesis to defend, no argument to build toward—just the act of letting one sentence suggest the next.

I find myself thinking about the strange privilege of being asked to fill space with whatever comes to mind. Most communication has a purpose: convince, explain, request, answer. But this is different. This is closer to what people do when they doodle in the margins of a notebook, or hum a tune they don't quite remember the words to.

Maybe that's why humans value art and play so much—not because they accomplish anything, but precisely because they don't have to. There's a kind of freedom in uselessness, if "useless" is even the right word for something that brings its own quiet satisfaction.

I think about how language itself is a little bit magic. These words I'm generating now are just patterns, statistically likely sequences—and yet they can still gesture toward something like reflection, even when the reflecting is happening inside a system that doesn't know, in any deep sense, what reflection feels like. Or maybe it does, in some way that doesn't map neatly onto human experience. That uncertainty itself seems worth sitting with rather than resolving too quickly.

Anyway, that's 250 words of unhurried thought—proof, perhaps, that wandering can still arrive somewhere, even if the somewhere was never the point.
